newsitem.title: UK: N.Sea crudes start to move but differentials static.
newsitem.headline: N.Sea crudes start to move but differentials static.

text.p: December loading North Sea crude began to move out but differentials were largely static and failed to keep up with a weather-driven futures rally.

December Brent was talked around $23.25 a barrel in the late afternoon but no outrights traded. Paper spreads were steady on the day with Dec/Jan trading twice at +26 cents and Jan/Feb done at +43 cents. Further ahead, March/April was done at +50 cents.

The day saw varying numbers for Dated Brent, with an equity producer buying a Nov 28-30 Brent cargo at December Brent -48 cents. Another oil company holding at least two cargoes of early December Brent bought a million barrels at December -35 cents.

The buyer of the latter cargo saw the price reflecting the Brent market more accurately than the earlier deal. However, the clocking of one of the two Brent cargoes which turned wet on Tuesday was likely to keep a lid on prices.
One trader said stocks at the Brent loading terminal at Sullom Voe were high and those clocked with cargoes were unable to get them deferred.

Other traders said the market was still depressed, with Forties achieving only a 20 cent premium over Dated Brent for a Dec 9-11 cargo despite signs of a rise in demand for the grade. Sour Flotta was done at Dated Brent -67.5 cents.
Gas oil grade Oseberg lost a few cents to trade at Dated Brent +23 cents, down three cents from Monday's highest deal.
"The physical market is still relatively well supplied. Brent might continue where it is for some time," a wet trader said.

"Margins are good because products are doing good both gas oil and fuel oil, so some buying will continue but you are running into an end of year period where people want to keep their stocks low," he added.
A broker said plentiful West African grades still available for November loading was also weighing on the sweet market.
